MEC-Cox implementation

A worked example following Supplement S2.4

  • Data and notation
  • Step 1. Construction of the cross-fitted predictor basis
  • Step 2. Baseline ATT odds weights
  • Step 3. Formulation of the primal problem
  • Step 4. Conversion to the dual problem
  • Step 5. Dual Newton solver
  • Step 6. Final MEC-Cox estimator
  • Algorithm summary
  • Agreement with fit_mec_cox()
  • Run or rebuild this manual

This manual follows Steps 1–6 of Supplement S2.4, “Computation of the MEC-Cox Estimator via the Dual Newton Solver,” in the same order and with the same notation. Each formula is followed by the R code that implements it. The example uses the package’s simulated data, logistic regression for source propensity, Cox regression for control survival, and the Kullback–Leibler (KL) generator. The general generator notation from the supplement is retained.

R Markdown source · Package repository

Data and notation

The source indicator is Ai=1A_i=1 for the treated cohort and Ai=0A_i=0 for external controls. Write ℐa={i:Ai=a}\mathcal I_a=\{i:A_i=a\} and na=|ℐa|n_a=|\mathcal I_a|. The observed follow-up time and event indicator are stored in time and event. The baseline covariates XiX_i are age, sex, and marker.

Supplement notation R object Meaning
AiA_i; ℐ0,ℐ1\mathcal I_0,\mathcal I_1 A; I0, I1 Source indicator and cohort row indices
KK; κ(i)\kappa(i) K; kappa Number of folds and each subject’s fold
t1,…,tLt_1,\ldots,t_L, L=p−1L=p-1 t_landmark; L, p Landmark times and number of calibration features
ĥi\widehat h_i row i of H Intercept and held-out control-survival predictions
π̂i,q̂i,d̂i\widehat\pi_i,\widehat q_i,\widehat d_i pi_hat, q_hat, d_hat Propensity, odds, and normalized baseline control weights
H0,H1,THH_0,H_1,T_H H0, H1, T_H Cohort-specific feature matrices and target totals
λ,F(λ),J(λ)\lambda,F(\lambda),J(\lambda) lambda, F, J Dual parameter, calibration residual, and Jacobian
ŵi,ω̃i\widehat w_i,\widetilde\omega_i w_hat, omega_tilde Calibrated control weights and final weights for all subjects

Data structure. Selected rows from the simulated example, with values rounded for display. The row index ii refers to the original dataset. time is the observed follow-up time; event is 1 for an observed event and 0 for right censoring.

library(mecCox)
library(survival)
data(example_external_controls)
dat <- example_external_controls

A <- dat$source
I0 <- which(A == 0L)
I1 <- which(A == 1L)
n <- nrow(dat)
n0 <- length(I0)
n1 <- length(I1)
dat$A <- A
X_names <- c("age", "sex", "marker")

K <- 5L
seed <- 2026L
t_landmark <- c(3, 6, 9, 12, 15)
L <- length(t_landmark)
p <- L + 1L

data.frame(treated = n1, external_controls = n0,
           folds = K, landmarks = L, calibration_features = p)
#>   treated external_controls folds landmarks calibration_features
#> 1     160               320     5         5                    6

Run the code chunks in order. The five landmark times are fixed for this example; the same times and folds will be used in the package comparison.

Step 1. Construction of the cross-fitted predictor basis

Partition the pooled sample into KK folds, stratified by AiA_i, and let κ(i)\kappa(i) identify the fold containing subject ii. For each fold kk, train the control-survival learner using only ℐ0∩𝒥(−k)\mathcal I_0\cap\mathcal J^{(-k)}, then predict survival for all subjects in the held-out fold 𝒥(k)\mathcal J^{(k)}. The calibration-feature vector is

ĥi=(1,Ŝ0(−κ(i))(t1∣Xi),…,Ŝ0(−κ(i))(tp−1∣Xi))∈ℝp. \widehat h_i= \left(1,\widehat S_0^{(-\kappa(i))}(t_1\mid X_i),\ldots, \widehat S_0^{(-\kappa(i))}(t_{p-1}\mid X_i)\right)\in\mathbb R^p.

Figure S1. Schematic illustration of KK-fold cross-fitting, reproduced from the supplement. Within each training set, the propensity learner uses both cohorts and the control-survival learner uses external controls only. Both are evaluated on subjects in the held-out fold.

For the Cox survival learner used here,

Ŝ0,Cox(−k)(tℓ∣Xi)=exp⁡[−Λ̂00(−k)(tℓ)exp{Xi⊤β̂0(−k)}]. \widehat S_{0,\mathrm{Cox}}^{(-k)}(t_\ell\mid X_i)= \exp\left[-\widehat\Lambda_{00}^{(-k)}(t_\ell) \exp\{X_i^\top\widehat\beta_0^{(-k)}\}\right]. 

set.seed(seed)
kappa <- integer(n)
for (a in c(0L, 1L)) {
  rows <- which(A == a)
  kappa[rows] <- sample(rep(seq_len(K), length.out = length(rows)))
}

S0_hat <- matrix(NA_real_, nrow = n, ncol = L)
survival_formula <- reformulate(X_names, response = "Surv(time, event)")

for (k in seq_len(K)) {
  train0 <- which(kappa != k & A == 0L)
  valid <- which(kappa == k)

  outcome_fit <- coxph(
    survival_formula, data = dat[train0, ],
    ties = "breslow", x = TRUE, singular.ok = FALSE,
    control = coxph.control(timefix = FALSE)
  )

  # Evaluate the baseline cumulative hazard at each landmark.
  baseline <- basehaz(outcome_fit, centered = FALSE)
  j <- findInterval(t_landmark, baseline$time)
  Lambda00_hat <- numeric(L)
  Lambda00_hat[j > 0L] <- baseline$hazard[j[j > 0L]]

  # Uncentered linear predictors match the uncentered baseline hazard.
  lp <- predict(outcome_fit, newdata = dat[valid, ],
                type = "lp", reference = "zero")
  S0_hat[valid, ] <- exp(-outer(exp(lp), Lambda00_hat))
}

colnames(S0_hat) <- paste0("S0(t=", t_landmark, ")")
H <- cbind(intercept = 1, S0_hat)
stopifnot(all(is.finite(H)), all(S0_hat >= 0 & S0_hat <= 1))
head(H, 3)
#>      intercept  S0(t=3)  S0(t=6)  S0(t=9) S0(t=12) S0(t=15)
#> [1,]         1 0.779711 0.601856 0.406193 0.310231 0.236855
#> [2,]         1 0.940462 0.872949 0.796002 0.754639 0.703516
#> [3,]         1 0.786413 0.612459 0.418977 0.322975 0.248884

Each row is predicted without using that subject to train the survival model. These predictions enter the calibration features; the final Cox model in Step 6 uses the source indicator AiA_i as its sole regression covariate.

Step 2. Baseline ATT odds weights

Using the same folds, fit the source propensity model on the pooled training sample 𝒥(−k)\mathcal J^{(-k)}. Evaluate it on 𝒥(k)\mathcal J^{(k)} to obtain π̂i=π̂(−k)(Xi)\widehat\pi_i=\widehat\pi^{(-k)}(X_i). For i∈ℐ0i\in\mathcal I_0, form

q̂i=π̂i1−π̂i,d̂i=n1q̂i∑j∈ℐ0q̂j,∑i∈ℐ0d̂i=n1. \widehat q_i=\frac{\widehat\pi_i}{1-\widehat\pi_i}, \qquad \widehat d_i=\frac{n_1\widehat q_i} {\sum_{j\in\mathcal I_0}\widehat q_j}, \qquad \sum_{i\in\mathcal I_0}\widehat d_i=n_1. 

pi_hat <- numeric(n)
propensity_formula <- reformulate(X_names, response = "A")

for (k in seq_len(K)) {
  train <- which(kappa != k)
  valid <- which(kappa == k)
  propensity_fit <- glm(propensity_formula, data = dat[train, ],
                        family = binomial())
  stopifnot(isTRUE(propensity_fit$converged))
  pi_hat[valid] <- predict(propensity_fit, newdata = dat[valid, ],
                           type = "response")
}

ps_trim <- c(0.01, 0.99)
pi_hat <- pmin(pmax(pi_hat, ps_trim[1]), ps_trim[2])
q_hat <- pi_hat[I0] / (1 - pi_hat[I0])
d_hat <- n1 * q_hat / sum(q_hat)

stopifnot(all(is.finite(d_hat)), all(d_hat > 0))
c(baseline_weight_total = sum(d_hat), treated_count = n1)
#> baseline_weight_total         treated_count
#>                   160                   160

The truncation bounds are explicit so that the hand calculation and the package use the same propensity scores. d_hat contains external-control weights only, in the order specified by I0.

Step 3. Formulation of the primal problem

Stack the rows ĥi\widehat h_i within each cohort to obtain H0∈ℝn0×pH_0\in\mathbb R^{n_0\times p} and H1∈ℝn1×pH_1\in\mathbb R^{n_1\times p}. The target calibration total is

TH=H1⊤𝟏n1=∑i∈ℐ1ĥi∈ℝp. T_H=H_1^\top\mathbf 1_{n_1} =\sum_{i\in\mathcal I_1}\widehat h_i\in\mathbb R^p.

The primal problem is

ŵ=arg⁡min{wi>0:i∈ℐ0}∑i∈ℐ0DG(wi∥d̂i)subject toH0⊤w=TH, \widehat w=\arg\min_{\{w_i>0:i\in\mathcal I_0\}} \sum_{i\in\mathcal I_0}D_G(w_i\|\widehat d_i) \quad\text{subject to}\quad H_0^\top w=T_H,

where DG(wi∥d̂i)=G(wi)−G(d̂i)−g(d̂i)(wi−d̂i)D_G(w_i\|\widehat d_i)=G(w_i)-G(\widehat d_i) -g(\widehat d_i)(w_i-\widehat d_i), GG is strictly convex, and g=G′g=G'. The intercept constraint preserves the total external-control weight n1n_1; the other constraints match the treated cohort’s predicted-survival totals.

H0 <- H[I0, , drop = FALSE]
H1 <- H[I1, , drop = FALSE]
T_H <- colSums(H1)

# KL generator from the manuscript: G(u) = u log(u), for u > 0.
G <- function(u) u * log(u)
g <- function(u) 1 + log(u)
g_inv <- function(v) exp(v - 1)
g_prime <- function(u) 1 / u

data.frame(feature = colnames(H),
           treated_total = T_H,
           baseline_control_total = as.numeric(crossprod(H0, d_hat)),
           row.names = NULL)
#>     feature treated_total baseline_control_total
#> 1 intercept      160.0000               160.0000
#> 2   S0(t=3)      140.4550               140.9055
#> 3   S0(t=6)      122.9990               123.6722
#> 4   S0(t=9)      104.3938               105.3782
#> 5  S0(t=12)       94.0362                95.0081
#> 6  S0(t=15)       83.2960                84.4723

We form this problem explicitly, then solve its pp-dimensional dual instead of optimizing over n0n_0 weights.

Step 4. Conversion to the dual problem

Use the same Lagrangian sign as the supplement:

ℒ(w,λ)=∑i∈ℐ0DG(wi∥d̂i)−λ⊤(H0⊤w−TH). \mathcal L(w,\lambda)=\sum_{i\in\mathcal I_0}D_G(w_i\|\widehat d_i) -\lambda^\top(H_0^\top w-T_H).

Stationarity gives g(wi)=g(d̂i)+λ⊤ĥig(w_i)=g(\widehat d_i)+\lambda^\top\widehat h_i, hence

wi(λ)=g−1{g(d̂i)+λ⊤ĥi},F(λ)=H0⊤w(λ)−TH=0. w_i(\lambda)=g^{-1}\{g(\widehat d_i)+\lambda^\top\widehat h_i\}, \qquad F(\lambda)=H_0^\top w(\lambda)-T_H=0.

This is the dual estimating equation. For the KL choice above, g(u)=1+log⁡ug(u)=1+\log u and g−1(v)=exp⁡(v−1)g^{-1}(v)=\exp(v-1), so wi(λ)=d̂iexp⁡(λ⊤ĥi)w_i(\lambda)=\widehat d_i\exp(\lambda^\top\widehat h_i).

w_of_lambda <- function(lambda) {
  nu <- g(d_hat) + as.numeric(H0 %*% lambda)
  g_inv(nu)
}

F <- function(lambda) {
  as.numeric(crossprod(H0, w_of_lambda(lambda)) - T_H)
}

lambda0 <- numeric(p)
stopifnot(max(abs(w_of_lambda(lambda0) - d_hat)) < 1e-12)

Step 5. Dual Newton solver

Define νi(λ)=g(d̂i)+λ⊤ĥi\nu_i(\lambda)=g(\widehat d_i)+\lambda^\top\widehat h_i. The dual domain contains values of λ\lambda for which every νi(λ)\nu_i(\lambda) belongs to dom⁡(g−1)\operatorname{dom}(g^{-1}). The Jacobian and Newton update are

J(λ)=H0⊤diag⁡[1g′{wi(λ)}:i∈ℐ0]H0, J(\lambda)=H_0^\top\operatorname{diag} \left[\frac{1}{g'\{w_i(\lambda)\}}:i\in\mathcal I_0\right]H_0, {J(λm)+ρIp}Δm=F(λm),λm+1=λm−αmΔm. \{J(\lambda_m)+\rho I_p\}\Delta_m=F(\lambda_m), \qquad \lambda_{m+1}=\lambda_m-\alpha_m\Delta_m.

For KL, 1/g′(wi)=wi1/g'(w_i)=w_i. The code uses the supplement’s choices ρ=10−8\rho=10^{-8}, ε=10−10\varepsilon=10^{-10}, and at most 100 Newton updates. Each update starts with αm=1\alpha_m=1. KL has dom⁡(g−1)=ℝ\operatorname{dom}(g^{-1})=\mathbb R; the step-halving guard below also rejects weights that overflow or underflow in finite-precision arithmetic. Convergence requires ∥F(λ̂)∥2≤ε\|F(\widehat\lambda)\|_2\le\varepsilon.

J <- function(lambda) {
  w <- w_of_lambda(lambda)
  crossprod(H0, H0 * (1 / g_prime(w)))
}

rho <- 1e-8
epsilon <- 1e-10
max_iter <- 100L
lambda <- lambda0
converged <- FALSE
history <- data.frame(iteration = integer(), residual_L2 = numeric())

for (m in 0:max_iter) {
  residual <- F(lambda)
  residual_L2 <- sqrt(sum(residual^2))
  history <- rbind(history, data.frame(iteration = m,
                                      residual_L2 = residual_L2))
  if (is.finite(residual_L2) && residual_L2 <= epsilon) {
    converged <- TRUE
    break
  }
  if (m == max_iter) break

  Delta <- solve(J(lambda) + rho * diag(p), residual)
  alpha <- 1
  accepted <- FALSE
  for (halving in 0:60) {
    candidate <- lambda - alpha * Delta
    w_candidate <- w_of_lambda(candidate)
    if (all(is.finite(w_candidate)) && all(w_candidate > 0)) {
      accepted <- TRUE
      break
    }
    alpha <- alpha / 2
  }
  if (!accepted) stop("No admissible Newton step was found.")
  lambda <- candidate
}

if (!converged) stop("The dual solver did not reach the stated tolerance.")
lambda_hat <- lambda
w_hat <- w_of_lambda(lambda_hat)
history
#>   iteration residual_L2
#> 1         0 1.98840e+00
#> 2         1 3.02732e+00
#> 3         2 5.82436e-02
#> 4         3 3.65760e-05
#> 5         4 1.96874e-11

The balance table makes the constraint H0⊤ŵ=THH_0^\top\widehat w=T_H visible.

knitr::kable(data.frame(
  feature = colnames(H),
  treated_mean = T_H / n1,
  baseline_control_mean = as.numeric(crossprod(H0, d_hat)) / n1,
  calibrated_control_mean = as.numeric(crossprod(H0, w_hat)) / n1
), digits = 6, row.names = FALSE,
col.names = c("Feature", "Treated mean", "Baseline control mean",
              "Calibrated control mean"))
Feature Treated mean Baseline control mean Calibrated control mean
intercept 1.000000 1.000000 1.000000
S0(t=3) 0.877844 0.880659 0.877844
S0(t=6) 0.768744 0.772951 0.768744
S0(t=9) 0.652461 0.658614 0.652461
S0(t=12) 0.587726 0.593801 0.587726
S0(t=15) 0.520600 0.527952 0.520600

Step 6. Final MEC-Cox estimator

Recover ŵi=g−1{g(d̂i)+λ̂⊤ĥi}\widehat w_i=g^{-1}\{g(\widehat d_i)+\widehat\lambda^\top\widehat h_i\} for external controls. The final estimating-equation weights are

ω̃i=Ai+(1−Ai)ŵi. \widetilde\omega_i=A_i+(1-A_i)\widehat w_i.

Treated subjects retain weight one. Using these weights, define

SMEC,ω(r)(t;θ)=∑i=1nω̃i𝒴i(t)exp⁡(θAi)Air,r=0,1, S_{\mathrm{MEC},\omega}^{(r)}(t;\theta) =\sum_{i=1}^n\widetilde\omega_i\mathcal Y_i(t) \exp(\theta A_i)A_i^r,\qquad r=0,1, A¯MEC,ω(t;θ)=SMEC,ω(1)(t;θ)SMEC,ω(0)(t;θ). \overline A_{\mathrm{MEC},\omega}(t;\theta) =\frac{S_{\mathrm{MEC},\omega}^{(1)}(t;\theta)} {S_{\mathrm{MEC},\omega}^{(0)}(t;\theta)}.

Here 𝒴i(t)\mathcal Y_i(t) is the at-risk indicator and 𝒩i(t)\mathcal N_i(t) is the event counting process. Solve

UnMEC(θ)=∑i=1n∫ω̃i{Ai−A¯MEC,ω(t;θ)}d𝒩i(t)=0 U_n^{\mathrm{MEC}}(\theta)=\sum_{i=1}^n\int\widetilde\omega_i \{A_i-\overline A_{\mathrm{MEC},\omega}(t;\theta)\}\,d\mathcal N_i(t)=0

and report HR̂MEC=exp⁡(θ̂MEC)\widehat{\mathrm{HR}}_{\mathrm{MEC}}=\exp(\widehat\theta_{\mathrm{MEC}}). In R, the point estimate is obtained by fitting a weighted Cox model with A as its sole covariate. Breslow handling of tied events matches the package.

omega_tilde <- rep(1, n)
omega_tilde[I0] <- w_hat
dat$omega_tilde <- omega_tilde

final_fit <- coxph(
  Surv(time, event) ~ A, data = dat, weights = omega_tilde,
  ties = "breslow", robust = FALSE,
  control = coxph.control(timefix = FALSE)
)
theta_hat <- unname(coef(final_fit)["A"])
HR_hat <- exp(theta_hat)
data.frame(log_hazard_ratio = theta_hat, hazard_ratio = HR_hat)
#>   log_hazard_ratio hazard_ratio
#> 1        0.0899067      1.09407

This step illustrates the point estimator. For the MEC stacked-sandwich standard error and confidence interval, use fit_mec_cox() as below; the ordinary weighted coxph() standard error is not that variance estimator.

Algorithm summary

Algorithm S1. Computational algorithm for the MEC-Cox estimator

  1. Partition the pooled sample into KK folds, stratified by the source indicator AiA_i.

  2. For each validation subject i∈𝒥(k)i\in\mathcal J^{(k)}, compute cross-fitted nuisance estimates

    π̂i=π̂(−k)(Xi),ĥi=(1,Ŝ0(−k)(t1∣Xi),…,Ŝ0(−k)(tp−1∣Xi)), \widehat\pi_i=\widehat\pi^{(-k)}(X_i), \qquad \widehat h_i= \left(1,\widehat S_0^{(-k)}(t_1\mid X_i),\ldots, \widehat S_0^{(-k)}(t_{p-1}\mid X_i)\right),

    where π̂(−k)\widehat\pi^{(-k)} is trained on 𝒥(−k)\mathcal J^{(-k)}, and Ŝ0(−k)\widehat S_0^{(-k)} is trained using external controls in ℐ0∩𝒥(−k)\mathcal I_0\cap\mathcal J^{(-k)}.

  3. For i∈ℐ0i\in\mathcal I_0, define the normalized baseline ATT odds weight

    d̂i=n1q̂i∑j∈ℐ0q̂j,q̂i=π̂i1−π̂i. \widehat d_i= \frac{n_1\widehat q_i}{\sum_{j\in\mathcal I_0}\widehat q_j}, \qquad \widehat q_i=\frac{\widehat\pi_i}{1-\widehat\pi_i}.

  4. Solve the dual calibration equation

    F(λ)=∑i∈ℐ0ĥig−1{g(d̂i)+λ⊤ĥi}−∑i∈ℐ1ĥi=0 F(\lambda)= \sum_{i\in\mathcal I_0} \widehat h_i g^{-1}\{g(\widehat d_i)+\lambda^\top\widehat h_i\} -\sum_{i\in\mathcal I_1}\widehat h_i=0

    by a damped Newton solver, and denote the solution by λ̂\widehat\lambda.

  5. Recover the MEC-updated external-control weights and the final estimating-equation weights:

    ŵi=g−1{g(d̂i)+λ̂⊤ĥi},ω̃i=ωi(λ̂)=Ai+(1−Ai)ŵi. \widehat w_i= g^{-1}\{g(\widehat d_i)+\widehat\lambda^\top\widehat h_i\}, \qquad \widetilde\omega_i= \omega_i(\widehat\lambda)= A_i+(1-A_i)\widehat w_i.

  6. Report HR̂MEC=exp⁡(θ̂MEC)\widehat{\mathrm{HR}}_{\mathrm{MEC}}=\exp(\widehat\theta_{\mathrm{MEC}}) by solving

    UnMEC(θ)=∑i=1n∫ω̃i{Ai−A¯MEC,ω(t;θ)}d𝒩i(t)=0. U_n^{\mathrm{MEC}}(\theta)= \sum_{i=1}^n\int\widetilde\omega_i \{A_i-\overline A_{\mathrm{MEC},\omega}(t;\theta)\} \,d\mathcal N_i(t)=0.

Algorithm lines 1–3 construct the inputs developed in Steps 1–2 above; line 4 combines Steps 3–5; and lines 5–6 give the final calculation in Step 6.

Agreement with fit_mec_cox()

The package call performs these calculations together. We supply the same learners, folds, landmark times, and propensity bounds used above.

mec <- fit_mec_cox(
  example_external_controls,
  time = "time", event = "event", source = "source",
  covariates = X_names, ps_learner = "glm", survival_learner = "cox",
  n_folds = K, landmarks = t_landmark, seed = seed, ps_trim = ps_trim
)

# First verify the ingredients, before comparing the calibrated estimates.
stopifnot(
  identical(kappa, mec$fold_id),
  max(abs(pi_hat - mec$ps_oof)) < 1e-12,
  max(abs(H - mec$basis)) < 1e-12,
  max(abs(d_hat - mec$baseline_weights[I0])) < 1e-12
)

knitr::kable(data.frame(
  calculation = c("Steps 1-6", "fit_mec_cox()"),
  log_hazard_ratio = c(theta_hat, mec$theta),
  hazard_ratio = c(HR_hat, mec$hr),
  control_weight_total = c(sum(w_hat), sum(mec$weights[I0])),
  max_mean_balance_residual = format(
    c(max(abs(F(lambda_hat))) / n1,
      mec$calibration$max_mean_balance_residual), scientific = TRUE, digits = 3
  )
), digits = 6,
col.names = c("Calculation", "Log HR", "HR", "Control weight total",
              "Max. mean residual"))
Calculation Log HR HR Control weight total Max. mean residual
Steps 1-6 0.089907 1.09407 160 8.42e-14
fit_mec_cox() 0.089907 1.09407 160 8.46e-14 
stopifnot(max(abs(w_hat - mec$weights[I0])) < 1e-5,
          abs(theta_hat - mec$theta) < 1e-7)

The worked solver uses S2.4’s numerical choices. The package solves the same KL balance equation using a scaled ridge, a dual-objective line search, and calibration_tol applied to max⁡|F|/n1\max|F|/n_1 (default 10−810^{-8}). Accordingly, the comparison checks numerical agreement rather than identical iterations. The public fit_mec_cox() implementation uses KL calibration; the supplement’s general GG notation also describes other generators.

For routine analysis, the package also returns the MEC uncertainty estimates:

data.frame(hazard_ratio = mec$hr, SE_log_hazard_ratio = mec$se,
           CI_lower = unname(mec$conf_int["lower"]),
           CI_upper = unname(mec$conf_int["upper"]))
#>   hazard_ratio SE_log_hazard_ratio CI_lower CI_upper
#> 1      1.09407            0.135446 0.838986  1.42672
